entries.note:
The colour channels blend `src.a, 1-src.a`; the ALPHA channel blends `1, 1-src.a`. Setting both to plain alpha would multiply the destination's alpha by the source's coverage a second time, so the composited alpha of overlapping translucent controls drifts low with each layer.

**This is invisible in the render spec**, and that is worth knowing before anyone 'simplifies' it. The snapshot path reads RGB out of an opaque framebuffer, so a wrong destination alpha changes no asserted pixel. It was ported because `backend_gl.c` had always asked GL for exactly this (`glBlendFuncSeparate(SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA, ONE, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA)`) and the port's rule was to move no arithmetic — not because a test defends it. It is the same untestable-by-pixels category spec 123 records for the buffer usage hint.

entries.note:
This was `backend_gl.c`'s bottom-left expression, carried over with a comment claiming the seam had made the origin uniform across backends. **It had not.** Vulkan's `VkRect2D` and Metal's `MTLScissorRect` are measured from the top, OpenGL's from the bottom, and the seam handed each API these numbers unchanged — so the Metal copy drew every pane's clip upside down the first time one existed.

The seam's header now states top-left, matching `re_seam_texture_update`, and the OpenGL backend converts using the bound target's height. Nothing in the repository could have caught the disagreement beforehand: every caller clipped either the full height or nothing.

Removing the OpenGL conversion is a sabotage worth knowing is caught — 212,381 pixels outside the 2px band on the workspace scene — so this expression can stay a plain scale.

A 2048-square atlas is 4 MiB at one byte a pixel and 16 MiB at four. `backend_gl.c` kept glyph coverage in a `GL_RED` page; the seam had only RGBA until this port asked for it, which is how `RE_SEAM_TEXTURE_COVERAGE` came to exist — the third API gap found by writing a real consumer rather than imagining one, after the render target and the packed-byte attribute.

A sabotage that makes the page RGBA internally **cannot** be caught by any pixel test: GL expands R to (r, 0, 0, 1), the shader's `.r` survives, and the frame is identical. What it costs is 12 MiB.

entries.note:
Twelve bytes saved per vertex across a 65,536-vertex batch is 768 KiB of upload per full batch. This is why the seam grew `RE_SEAM_ATTRIBUTE_UNORM8` as a second attribute type rather than letting the draw list widen four bytes into four floats on the way in.

The shader reads it as normalised, so `ui.glsl` sees the same `vec4` in 0..1 it would have seen from floats — the layout change is invisible above the attribute declaration, which is the property that let this be a port rather than a rewrite.

Everything below the draw list that knows a graphics API lives in `seam_host_*.c`; this file reaches one through `seam_host.h` and otherwise calls only the pack. `tools/design.py`'s `native_render_layering` enforces that — it allows API symbols in `render/backend_*.c` and `render/seam_host_*.c` and nowhere else, and `backend_seam.c` is a `backend_` file only by name, carrying none.

Keeping it true is what makes the eventual three prefixed seam copies a link-time question (spec 126 decision 3) instead of a source one.

That stayed true, and it is what made the three prefixed copies a LINK-time question rather than a source one: this file is compiled once per graphics API with a rename header force-included, and the only thing that differs between the copies is which seam and which `seam_host_*.c` they were linked against. `ops.name` is written from the host's own name at open because there is no other way for one source, compiled three times, to say which copy it is — and since the hand-written backends were deleted, that name IS the `--renderer` value: opengl, vulkan or metal.
